title: Quantifying the risk of caesarean sections on a uterine rupture in pregnant women between 24 and 42 weeks` gestation undergoing a planned or unplanned caesarean section – a retrospective, single centre case-control study in a tertiary care facility
summary: A uterine rupture is a tear of the wall of the womb in pregnant women describing a situation that is potentially deadly for mother and child. A scarred womb is known to be associated with this condition. There is the problematic trend that more planned surgical deliveries are carried out, especially in women who have never given birth before. This trend increases the number of women with a scarred womb making them vulnerable during pregnancy. Most will choose a repeat surgical delivery, mostly out of fear of a tear. This vicious circle is bad for patients and the health sector in terms of costs. The study aims to provide reliable and understandable evidence to health care professionals and patients on the consequences and complications of surgical deliveries in following pregnancies. Through improved consultations, the study tries to reduce the number of planned surgical deliveries in low-risk pregnancies, expecting better medical care for patients and lower costs for the health sector.
conditions: Rupture of uterus before onset of labour

interventions.name: No uterine rupture patients for the control group from 2010 to 2025, considering given matching criteria.
Cases with a uterine rupture between the years 2010 and 2025.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Women with a singleton pregnancy aged 18 and above who meet the criteria of a planned or unplanned caesarean section with at least 1 prior c-section in their medical history will be recruited. They will be between 23+0- and 42+0-weeks’ gestation.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients will be ineligible to be included if they have a history of maternal congenital uterine malformations or critical illnesses that may not allow them to make autonomous decisions. A potential participant is ineligible if there is doubt that the individual was able to understand the circumstances, express a preference or act freely. An individual is also deemed ineligible on those grounds if a health care proxy is involved.
